clue.text: Stop consuming German sausage loudly — it's what losers do

parts.note: to come off a drug or medicine is to stop taking it

indicators.note: spoken out loud, one word is heard as another that sounds the same

parts.note: wurst is the German word for sausage, said like the English word for least good

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to quit wolfing down bratwurst noisily, with a jibe that such behaviour marks a loser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loudly' signals the sound-alike: WURST spoken out loud is heard as WORST.
explanation.definitionFit: To come off worst is to be beaten in a contest, which is exactly the outcome for those who lose.

clue.text: Apple computer programming absorbs learner

indicators.note: something that absorbs another takes it into itself, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: coding is writing computer programs
L is the learner plate on a British car

explanation.surface: An Apple machine's software courses take in a student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple computer' reads as the tech brand; the definition is just 'Apple', the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A codling is a variety of cooking apple, a long, tapering type grown in England.

clue.text: Concerning a union, almost spoil the entire thing

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil it

indicators.note: almost means the phrase stops just short, its last letter dropped

parts.note: it all means everything, the entire thing

explanation.surface: A warning that a single problem within a partnership can nearly ruin everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims the final L from IT ALL, giving ITAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Marital means relating to marriage, the union of a wedded couple.

clue.text: Forged euros sold, not creating a stink

indicators.note: forged things are fakes, made anew, so these letters are recast into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Counterfeit currency was traded quietly, without raising any outcry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forged' rearranges EUROS and SOLD together. 'creating a stink' looks like making a fuss, but here it is a literal smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Odourless means having no smell at all, so it gives off no stink.

clue.text: Providing revolutionary service for meat dish

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns over, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: if means providing, on condition that
a let is a tennis serve that clips the net and is replayed

explanation.surface: A radical restaurant service supplying a meat course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' signals the turnaround. A let is a tennis serve that clips the net and is replayed.
explanation.definitionFit: A filet is a boneless cut of meat or fish, the French form of fillet, served as a dish on menus.

clue.text: When we say goodbye, not stopping

parts.note: on can mean when, as in on arrival, at the time of
we say goodbye on going, when departing

explanation.surface: Farewells that never quite end.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'on going': at the moment of leaving is when goodbyes are said.
explanation.definitionFit: Ongoing means continuing without a halt, still in progress.

clue.text: Try overturning ram in field event

parts.note: a shot is an attempt or try

indicators.note: in a down answer, overturning turns the word upside down, so its letters read backwards

parts.note: a tup is a ram, a male sheep

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to tip over a ram in a pasture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturning' flips TUP to PUT. 'field' suggests farmland for the ram, but it is athletics.
explanation.definitionFit: The shot put is an athletics field event in which a heavy metal ball is thrown for distance.

clue.text: Thinkers with urge to move around fast

indicators.note: moving letters around shuffles them into a new order

explanation.surface: Philosophers itching to get moving quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move around' is the anagram signal. 'fast' looks like speed but is the noun: going without food.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunger strike is a fast, refusing food as a protest.

clue.text: Perform inadequately, caught by all-rounder D'Oliveira

indicators.note: the answer is caught, held within the run of letters of these words

explanation.surface: A cricketer underperforms after being caught off Basil D'Oliveira, the England all-rounder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught by' holds the answer inside all-roUNDER DOliveira. 'caught by' sounds like a cricket dismissal. Basil D'Oliveira was a South African-born England cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: To underdo is to do something less thoroughly than needed, falling short in performance.

clue.text: In France, the man of the match is in space

parts.note: le is French for the
the groom is the man being matched, at a wedding

explanation.surface: A French sporting star is given room to manoeuvre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of the match' suggests a sports award; here the match is a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Legroom is space for the legs, as in a car or aircraft seat.

clue.text: Wise partner on horse in English coastal area

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: Eric Morecambe was the comedy partner of Ernie Wise
a bay is a reddish-brown horse

explanation.surface: A sensible companion rides a horse along the English shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe and Wise were a much-loved British TV comedy double act; 'Wise' looks like an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Morecambe Bay is a large estuary bay on the north-west coast of England, famous for its tides.

clue.text: Be brilliant in golf, then rubbish

parts.note: G is golf in the radio alphabet
litter is rubbish dropped in public

explanation.surface: A golfer shines on the course, then makes a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: To glitter is to shine with bright, sparkling light, which is to be brilliant.

clue.text: Tourist double parking in German city

indicators.note: one piece goes in, inside, the other here

parts.note: Trier is an ancient city in western Germany

indicators.note: double asks for the parking letter to be given twice over, side by side

parts.note: P is the map symbol for parking

explanation.surface: A visitor parks illegally, side by side with another car, in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double parking' reads as a motoring offence; 'in' puts the pair inside the city name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tripper is someone on a day trip or outing, a holidaymaker or sightseer.

clue.text: Majestic king, for example Albert

parts.note: R stands for rex, Latin for king
Al is a short form of the name Albert

explanation.surface: A royal personage, such as Prince Albert, carries majesty.
explanation.definitionFit: Regal means kingly or royal in bearing, befitting a monarch.

clue.text: Mention coming back on green, struggling with drive

indicators.note: in an across answer, a piece on another follows it
letters that are struggling are thrashing about, out of order
coming back means this word is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: to cite is to mention or quote

explanation.surface: A golfer brings up, back on the putting green, trouble with a tee shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' is the anagram signal and 'coming back' the turnaround; 'on' in an across clue puts the second part after. 'green' and 'drive' look like golf.
explanation.definitionFit: Energetic means full of energy and vigour, having plenty of drive.

clue.text: Reformed sinners he holds sacred

indicators.note: reformed things are made over in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man who has turned former wrongdoers to good keeps them in reverence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed' rearranges SINNERS and HE together.
explanation.definitionFit: To enshrine something is to cherish it as sacred, as if placing it in a shrine.

clue.text: One good cutting hair for catty females

indicators.note: one piece cutting another goes into it, splitting it

parts.note: tresses are long locks of hair
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A decent hairdresser trims locks for some spiteful women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' puts I and G inside TRESSES. 'catty' reads as spiteful, but is literally cat-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Tigresses are female tigers, literally female members of the cat family.

clue.text: Family member has a thousand pounds per year

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds
p.a. is per annum, Latin for per year

explanation.surface: A relative earns a thousand pounds a year.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandpa is a grandfather, a relative two generations up.

clue.text: Great example of mathematical ratio in e-book

indicators.note: one piece goes in, inside, the other here

parts.note: an electronic tome, a tome being a large book
pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter

explanation.surface: An electronic textbook gives a fine example of a mathematical ratio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'e-book' splits into the letter E plus a word for a large book.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is a perfect representative or embodiment, a supreme instance of a type.

clue.text: Sultanas extracted from Danish are mushy

indicators.note: the answer is extracted, pulled out from the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: The dried fruit picked out of Danish pastries has gone soggy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extracted from' finds the answer in daniSH ARE Mushy. 'Sultanas' reads as dried grapes but means the wives of a sultan.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the women of a sultan's household, so they are, punningly, the sultan's sultanas.

clue.text: Travelling bag in ancient lobby, according to Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

parts.note: old means ancient
a hall is an entrance lobby

explanation.surface: A holdall is spotted in an antique entrance hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'according to Spooner' moves the H of HALL to the front of OLD, giving HOLD ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A holdall is a large soft bag for carrying clothes and belongings on a journey.

clue.text: All are excited, drinking energy drink in pubs

indicators.note: something drinking another takes it in, so one piece goes inside the other
excited letters are stirred up, so these are put into a new order

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Everyone is thrilled, knocking back an energy drink at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges ALL ARE and 'drinking' takes E inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Real ale is traditionally brewed cask beer, a drink served in British pubs.

clue.text: Characters displaying a certain inclination?

parts.note: characters are printed letters, and their inclination is a literal slant to the right, not a leaning of personality

explanation.surface: People in a story who reveal a particular tendency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests people with leanings; here they are letters in a slanted typeface.
explanation.definitionFit: Italics are a sloping style of type, letters that lean to the right.

clue.text: Second part of tennis match, losing with a fight

parts.note: a set is a division of a tennis match

indicators.note: losing means a letter is dropped from the phrase

parts.note: second is number two

explanation.surface: A tennis player drops the second set amid a heated argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes W from TWO. 'Second part of tennis match' reads as one phrase, set two.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is a short, sharp quarrel or brawl.

clue.text: Empty residence let for free

indicators.note: an empty word has its insides removed, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: to lease is to let out property

explanation.surface: A vacant house is rented out without charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' keeps RE from residence. 'free' looks like no charge but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To release is to set free, letting someone or something go.

clue.text: Don't seem half-hearted, playing in final

indicators.note: letters playing are at play, moving freely into a new arrangement
half its heart goes, so one of the two central letters is removed

explanation.surface: A coach urges a team not to look lacklustre while competing in a final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' drops one E of the two at the centre of SEEM, leaving SEM; 'playing' rearranges DONT and SEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Endmost means furthest towards the end, the last in a sequence.

clue.text: Falls in this river?

parts.note: falls reads as a verb, someone tumbling in, but names a famous waterfall on the river

explanation.surface: A question about which river someone tumbled into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls' looks like a verb; it is the waterfall named after the river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Niagara is the river joining Lakes Erie and Ontario, whose waterfalls are among the most famous on Earth.

clue.text: French girl produced white wine around Italy

parts.note: made means produced

indicators.note: one piece goes around the other, enclosing it

parts.note: Moselle is a white wine from the Moselle valley
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A young Frenchwoman made white wine while touring Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts I inside MOSELLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mademoiselle is the French title for an unmarried woman, used for a young girl.
